title: Count the records
prompt: How many data records are in the NYC permits sheet? Exclude the header.
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. Count the identifier column and exclude the header.
rule: Count the identifier column and exclude the header.
code: =COUNTA(A2:A33503)

title: Missing ZIP codes
prompt: How many records have an empty ZipCode cell?
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. A missing ZIP code is different from an invalid or multiple ZIP code.
rule: A missing ZIP code is different from an invalid or multiple ZIP code.
code: =COUNTBLANK(N2:N33503)

title: Most common event
prompt: Which EventType occurs most often?
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. Use counts of records, not sums of identifier values.
rule: Use counts of records, not sums of identifier values.
code: Create a PivotTable: Rows = EventType; Values = Count of EventID. Sort descending.

title: Two conditions
prompt: How many Shooting Permit records are in Brooklyn?
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. COUNTIFS applies all conditions to the same row. Counting only Brooklyn includes other event types.
rule: COUNTIFS applies all conditions to the same row. Counting only Brooklyn includes other event types.
code: =COUNTIFS(B2:B33503,"Shooting Permit",H2:H33503,"Brooklyn")

title: Student films
prompt: How many shooting permits have Category equal to Student?
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. Inspect the actual category labels before choosing a condition.
rule: Inspect the actual category labels before choosing a condition.
code: =COUNTIFS(B2:B33503,"Shooting Permit",K2:K33503,"Student")

title: Permit duration
prompt: Find the mean shooting-permit duration in hours, rounded to the nearest half hour.
method: Use the original NYC_Film_Permits sheet. Excel date differences are in days: multiply by 24 for hours.
rule: Excel date differences are in days: multiply by 24 for hours.
code:
In O2: =(D2-C2)*24
Fill down. Then: =MROUND(AVERAGEIF(B2:B33503,"Shooting Permit",O2:O33503),0.5)

title: Invoice count
prompt: How many invoices are in Invoice?
method: COUNT(*) counts rows including rows with NULL in other fields.
rule: COUNT(*) counts rows including rows with NULL in other fields.
code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invoices FROM Invoice;

title: Above the threshold
prompt: How many invoices have Total strictly greater than 20?
method: Use > for strictly greater than. >= includes the boundary.
rule: Use > for strictly greater than. >= includes the boundary.
code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invoices FROM Invoice WHERE Total > 20;

title: Between two values
prompt: How many invoices have Total > 10 and Total < 20?
method: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Use strict inequalities when the question excludes them.
rule: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Use strict inequalities when the question excludes them.
code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invoices FROM Invoice WHERE Total > 10 AND Total < 20;

title: Country selection
prompt: How many invoices have BillingCountry in Brazil, Argentina or Chile?
method: IN matches any listed value. AND cannot require one field to equal three countries.
rule: IN matches any listed value. AND cannot require one field to equal three countries.
code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invoices FROM Invoice WHERE BillingCountry IN ('Brazil','Argentina','Chile');

title: Missing company names
prompt: How many customers have a non-NULL Company?
method: COUNT(column) excludes NULL; COUNT(*) counts every row.
rule: COUNT(column) excludes NULL; COUNT(*) counts every row.
code: SELECT COUNT(Company) AS customers FROM Customer;

title: Country revenue
prompt: Return the five billing countries with the highest total invoice value. Break ties alphabetically.
answer:
BillingCountry | Revenue
USA | 523.06
Canada | 303.96
France | 195.1
Brazil | 190.1
Germany | 156.48
method: GROUP BY defines one output row per country; sum invoice totals before ranking.
rule: GROUP BY defines one output row per country; sum invoice totals before ranking.
code: SELECT BillingCountry, ROUND(SUM(Total),2) AS Revenue FROM Invoice GROUP BY BillingCountry ORDER BY SUM(Total) DESC, BillingCountry LIMIT 5;

title: Downloaded albums
prompt: How many distinct albums appear in purchased invoice lines?
method: Count distinct album identifiers, not invoice lines or track identifiers.
rule: Count distinct album identifiers, not invoice lines or track identifiers.
code: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT t.AlbumId) AS albums FROM InvoiceLine AS l JOIN Track AS t ON l.TrackId=t.TrackId;

title: Find a silent JOIN error
prompt: A student sums Invoice.Total after joining Invoice to InvoiceLine on InvoiceId. Explain why the total is inflated and calculate the correct invoice revenue.
method: Invoice.Total is at invoice level. Joining to multiple lines repeats the invoice total. SUM(DISTINCT Total) is not a safe fix: different invoices can have equal totals.
rule: Invoice.Total is at invoice level. Joining to multiple lines repeats the invoice total. SUM(DISTINCT Total) is not a safe fix: different invoices can have equal totals.
code: SELECT ROUND(SUM(Total),2) AS Revenue FROM Invoice;

title: Join without guessing IDs
prompt: List Drake songs, ordered by name, without hard-coding an artist identifier.
answer:

method: Join the foreign key to the artist key, then filter the artist name.
rule: Join the foreign key to the artist key, then filter the artist name.
code: SELECT s.name FROM songs s JOIN artists a ON s.artist_id=a.id WHERE a.name='Drake' ORDER BY s.name;

title: Average tempo
prompt: Find the average tempo of all songs, to two decimals.
method: AVG gives the arithmetic mean of non-NULL values.
rule: AVG gives the arithmetic mean of non-NULL values.
code: SELECT ROUND(AVG(tempo),2) AS tempo FROM songs;

rule: Case 2 uses three-letter location codes. Do not assume this is true in Case 3.

rule: Validate uniqueness of the combined key in PreparerInfo and preserve the journal-line count after the lookup.

answer: Amount = Debit + Credit. Subtracting an already negative credit reverses its sign.

rule: Inspect the sign convention before applying an accounting formula.

title: A meaningful hourly rate
prompt: How should you calculate aggregate gross pay per hour for a job code?
answer: SUM(gross pay) / SUM(regular hours + overtime hours), for the same job code and year.
method: The simple mean of row-level pay rates weights small and large rows equally. Use the ratio of totals, and flag zero-hour denominators.
rule: The simple mean of row-level pay rates weights small and large rows equally. Use the ratio of totals, and flag zero-hour denominators.

title: Choose the observation
prompt: Before modelling total daily restaurant sales, what should one row represent?
answer: One observed sales date, with netTotal summed across menu items.
method: Aggregate netTotal by date using SUM. Join weather and game data by date; code dates absent from the supplied game schedule as gameDay=0. Keep only observed sales dates (do not invent zero-sales dates). Include an intercept.
rule: An average across products measures average item sales, not total restaurant sales.

title: Temperature association
prompt: Regress total daily netTotal on tmax with an intercept. Report the slope to two decimals.
answer: 7.58 dollars per degree Fahrenheit. n=312; p=0.007666; R²=0.0227.
method: Aggregate netTotal by date using SUM. Join weather and game data by date; code dates absent from the supplied game schedule as gameDay=0. Keep only observed sales dates (do not invent zero-sales dates). Include an intercept.
rule: This is an association in observational data; statistical significance alone does not establish causation.
code:
Y = daily SUM(netTotal)
X = tmax

title: Game-day association
prompt: Regress total daily netTotal on gameDay with an intercept. Report the slope to two decimals.
method: Aggregate netTotal by date using SUM. Join weather and game data by date; code dates absent from the supplied game schedule as gameDay=0. Keep only observed sales dates (do not invent zero-sales dates). Include an intercept.
rule: In a binary-predictor regression with an intercept, the slope is the mean outcome for group 1 minus the mean for group 0.
code:
Y = daily SUM(netTotal)
X = gameDay (1 = game, 0 = no game)

title: Interpret an interaction
prompt: In sales = b0 + b1 × prior_sales + b2 × gameDay + b3 × prior_sales × gameDay, what is the slope of prior_sales on a game day?
answer: b1 + b3. The slope on a non-game day is b1.
method: Aggregate netTotal by date using SUM. Join weather and game data by date; code dates absent from the supplied game schedule as gameDay=0. Keep only observed sales dates (do not invent zero-sales dates). Include an intercept.
rule: Including two predictors without their product term does not estimate this interaction.

title: Forecast information
prompt: Why should a seven-day-ahead forecast not use the realised temperature seven days ahead as if it were known today?
answer: It uses future information unavailable at the forecast date. Use an available weather forecast or a stated temperature scenario and explain uncertainty.
method: Aggregate netTotal by date using SUM. Join weather and game data by date; code dates absent from the supplied game schedule as gameDay=0. Keep only observed sales dates (do not invent zero-sales dates). Include an intercept.
rule: Only information available at prediction time belongs in an honest forecast.
